body.text: Hanawon is South Korea’s main resettlement facility for people coming from North Korea. Those who pass its security screening come to pick up new skills, like learning how to open a bank account, use a computer, or find a job. They also learn skills to earn a living, like caregiving, painting, even how to hang wallpaper.

But on a recent spring day, the sprawling complex sat almost completely empty. A South Korean official showed us a chart tracking the number of North Koreans who made it to the South. At its peak in 2009, some 3,000 North Koreans entered the South in a single year. The line plunged dramatically. Last year, just 224 arrived. This year the number is on track to be even lower.

When I visited, Hanawon felt less like a crash course in capitalism and more like a leafy college campus over summer break – homey, but empty. The dormitories looked surprisingly cozy. We met a soft-spoken computer instructor who was genuinely enthusiastic about his work helping “North Korea-born citizens,” as the staff called them, adjust to life in the South. We passed a few students in the halls, but otherwise there were remarkably few people around.

Hanawon isn’t empty because its mission succeeded, or because North Korea had become a more desirable place to live. It’s emptier because fewer people are making it out. The South Korean government has already announced plans to consolidate Hanawon’s two facilities in response to the dwindling arrivals.

Walking through Hanawon, thousands of miles from my life as a tech entrepreneur in Los Angeles, it dawned on me: North Korean defectors are disappearing and we may encounter a day when we get to the last defector.

I don’t mean that literally, of course – people will always find a way to escape. Take two of the most recent North Koreans to defect to the South: a pair of soldiers, deployed to fight alongside the Russian military before being captured by Ukraine. Both are said to have wanted to go to South Korea, not go back home. One reportedly attempted suicide when faced with capture. Their extraordinary journey – from North Korea to Russia’s frontlines to a POW camp in Ukraine and finally to South Korea – highlights just how circuitous, and dangerous, an escape from the country may be going forward.

The journey to freedom was never easy for North Koreans. Previously, defectors had to cross the Yalu or Tumen Rivers and into China. Because Beijing considers them “illegal economic migrants” and routinely sends those it arrests back to North Korea, they must avoid capture while making their way through China, often traveling thousands of miles to reach Southeast Asia or Mongolia before continuing to South Korea. With greater surveillance and tighter controls along North Korea’s border with China, fewer North Koreans are willing to take the risk.

“It’s true that the number of residents [of North Korea] actually willing to try has decreased,” a recent defector named Gyuri recalled. “It would be dishonest to say otherwise. In the past, even if you attempted to defect and something went wrong, there was still some possibility of surviving. Now, if you are caught, you can lose your life. So the barrier to even attempting it has become much higher.”

Gyuri’s own story is illuminating: She was a table tennis instructor whose teaching income dried up during the pandemic. Seeking a new line of work, she built a business that operated wooden fishing vessels. But a steady salary did not bring her fulfillment.

Living in a coastal town allowed her and her family to watch South Korean television broadcasts. The programs had a magnetic pull on her and motivated Gyuri, along with her mother and aunt, to defect – naturally, by wooden boat – in October 2023.

They were among the lucky ones. And their stories may be among the last ones the rest of us get to hear. The lack of firsthand testimonials will have profound consequences for how North Korea is perceived and how much we know about what goes on there.
A whole generation of Americans is growing up with a detached, even indifferent, view of North Korea.
A Potemkin Village in Pyongyang

When I visited Pyongyang in 2012, I felt like I’d been dropped into a Stalinist version of “The Truman Show.” My handlers took me bowling. We visited a hospital, and rode Pyongyang’s subway. I even visited a movie studio there and presented my host with a fake Oscar statuette I’d brought for my trip. (He smiled politely, but I could tell he didn’t want to be caught enjoying the gift too much.)

What I remember most vividly were the children – dutifully drawing at their school desks but careful not to look up at me. Their intense concentration seemed so unnatural and forced, as if looking at this foreign visitor would somehow violate the script they’d been handed.

That was the strange thing about visiting Pyongyang: The whole place felt simultaneously real and staged – more like a movie set than an actual city. The subway worked fine. The bowling alley obviously existed. And the children were real schoolchildren. It was just obvious that somebody had curated what I was allowed to see and what I could not.

Foreign visitors to authoritarian countries tend to flatter themselves into thinking they can see through the carefully staged agitprop and propaganda. In North Korea, that confidence evaporates upon stepping foot in the airport. You know right away you are being shown a Potemkin Village. You just have no idea what’s behind the walls.

That is where defectors have played a key role. North Korea always posed an information problem for the outside world. Foreign journalists do not roam its cities or countryside, interviewing locals at random. Researchers cannot carry out surveys. Western spies struggle to gather reliable intelligence about life inside the country. Tourism is almost nonexistent, to say the least, and is carefully stage-managed, like my trip.

Defectors thus become some of our last remaining independent eyewitnesses to life beyond the movie set. Sure, their stories were not always perfect. Some accounts relayed by refugees over the years have been challenged or corrected. But collectively, their stories give us a picture of North Korean life, even if only a snapshot in time.
What happens when we lose our firsthand narrators? The answer, unfolding in real time, is that the image of North Korea will become sanitized.
Rehabilitating Kim’s Image

For years, North Korea occupied a strange though prominent place in the Western imagination. Books exposing conditions inside the country became bestsellers. Human rights organizations documented its prison camps. Hollywood lampooned the Kim dynasty. By the 2010s, North Korea seemed almost impossible to ignore. Dennis Rodman turned up in Pyongyang. “The Interview,” a satire about assassinating North Korea’s Supreme Leader, was reported to have enraged the regime so much that U.S. officials blamed Pyongyang for a cyberattack against Sony Pictures.

My generation grew up with an almost cartoonish caricature of the country and its mercurial dynastic leadership. It was an impression that vacillated between imminent threat and “South Park” punchline. North Korea was depicted as a bizarre and frightening place, though still the subject of crude jokes. It was always treated as an anomaly in the annals of global politics and culture. A landmark United Nations investigation in 2014 detailing crimes against humanity committed by the regime cemented that image.
Today, something qualitatively has changed.

North Korea’s leadership has not become less repressive. If anything, from what we know, it has gone in the opposite direction, thanks to the lifeline it receives from China and Russia. A recent U.N. assessment found that state control has intensified over the past decade and that severe punishments, including the death penalty, are now handed out for offenses as minor as distributing foreign media.

The Kim regime is also no longer diplomatically isolated. Kim presides over a nuclear-armed state courted by major powers. Russia depends on North Korean munitions and troops to replenish its depleting stockpiles and ranks. China remains Pyongyang’s economic and diplomatic benefactor. Indeed, North Korea’s government has gained leverage from the renewed desire to divide the world into “spheres of influence.”

Even Washington has helped (perhaps unwittingly) squeegee Kim’s image. During his first term, U.S. President Donald Trump mocked Kim as “Little Rocket Man.” The White House later shifted tactics and held not one but three summits with North Korea’s leader.

Slowly, a different image of North Korea began to emerge in Western coverage: a plucky, even resilient country where ride-hailing apps, electric vehicles, and gleaming new skyscrapers and construction projects are resurrecting a once-moribund economy. This kind of information has value. North Korea should not be frozen in our minds as the famine-ravaged Stalinist basketcase of the 1990s and 2000s.

Yet we should not whitewash – or worse, normalize – what is still the most repressive regime in the world. Authoritarian leaders know this dynamic well. For them to win the public relations game, they do not need to persuade the rest of the world that their societies are free. All they need to do is make the old stories told about their repressive behavior feel stale.

A person who escaped North Korea in, say, 2006 can tell us something about North Korea in 2006, the same year the country would join the nuclear club. By 2026 or even 2036, that eye-witness testimony still matters for the historical record. But it will tell us precious little about what daily life is like there decades later. Societies change. Forms of repression – and resistance – change. Even dynastic dictatorships evolve.
Without new waves of arrivals, and their stories, our picture of North Korea will slowly become stuck in the past.
A Dearth of Storytellers

U.S. adversaries understand that in an age of AI and 24/7 social media, narrative is power. A case in point is the Iranian state-linked AI-generated Lego-style videos that went viral earlier this year. The Kim dynasty has spent decades perfecting a simple story about itself: North Korea is a nation, heroic and permanently under siege, surrounded by enemies, protected by a sacred revolutionary bloodline whose sacrifices alone preserve the country. The Korean War never officially ended. In Pyongyang’s retelling, neither did the emergency.
Every dictatorship is the main narrator of its own existence. What distinguishes the most durable ones is their ability to eliminate competing narratives and narrators.

That is what worries me about the silence and emptiness I encountered at Hanawon. The facility was built on the assumption that North Koreans would keep arriving. The classrooms, workshops, dorms, and labs all constitute an elaborate infrastructure for escapees, a small South Korean bureaucracy designed around the proposition that people would flee North Korea until the Koreas are reunified. Now the infrastructure remains, but the people are nowhere to be found.

The obvious response is to preserve as much testimony as possible while we still can. Governments, universities, NGOs, filmmakers, journalists, and philanthropies should be recording the oral histories of recent defectors in far greater depth, not simply asking them about missile programs or politics, but documenting ordinary life: work, marriage, food, jokes, family, childhood, fear.

The United States’ film industry also can play a role. Storytelling and giving voice to people suffering behind iron curtains is something that Hollywood once thrived at. “The Killing Fields,” a gripping film about massacres carried out by the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, was only made thanks to the intrepid reporting of a journalist and the survival story of his Cambodian fixer. The Oscar-winning film did not replace historical scholarship about Cambodia. Nor did it directly impact policy or save lives – it came out several years too late. But it brought the distant horror, however briefly, into public consciousness. The same is true of stories from the Soviet Union and other closed societies.

North Korea has benefited from Beijing’s censorship of any criticism. Celebrities seeking out causes to celebrate tend to ignore North Korea (or Taiwan or Tibet, for that matter) for fear of angering Beijing and hurting their careers (just ask Kylian Mbappe). Chris Fenton, a longtime Hollywood executive who helped open the Chinese market to American films, described the industry’s accommodation of Beijing bluntly in a recent essay: “We rewrote scripts, moved settings, and scrubbed content to satisfy Beijing’s censors.” He pointed to a striking consequence of Hollywood’s rose-tinted depictions of China: A recent Pew survey found China viewed more favorably than the United States across most of the 36 countries surveyed.

This is why the decline in defections should trouble us far beyond the Korean Peninsula. Governments are obsessed with information. They worry about disinformation, deepfakes, AI, and propaganda. But the most effective information operation may be much simpler: prevent independent information from escaping in the first place. Then wait.

Wait for memories to fade or for eye-witnesses to grow old. Wait for other crises to command the world’s attention. Eventually, people may stop asking what is happening within walled-off societies. We see a version of this happening in Myanmar, Turkmenistan, and other places.

At Hanawon, I kept thinking about the defectors who had once filled those classrooms. They crossed rivers, hid from Chinese police, and traveled thousands of miles through unfamiliar terrain, scared. They had left parents, loved ones, siblings, and children behind; they knew they might never see their families again.

All they had were their stories – one of the few ways the rest of us could see through the elaborate stage set I encountered in Pyongyang years ago. Their stories complicate the regime’s propaganda. They give names and faces to people otherwise forgotten or reduced to statistics. They remind us that behind the missiles, military parades, nuclear tests, and absurdist pageantry, millions of ordinary people go on living, but trapped. Theirs is a country where the freedoms most of us take for granted – to speak one’s mind or choose what to read or watch on television – are almost nonexistent.

Those voices are disappearing. A whole generation is growing up with a neutral, almost detached, view of North Korea. Meanwhile, older generations of Americans may be rethinking their previously staunch anti-communist suspicions given the White House’s warm words for the Kim regime. Trump’s willingness to engage Kim as a fellow head of state has already helped cement his image as a leader to be taken seriously.

North Korea has achieved a public relations coup without doling out hundreds of millions for pricey PR firms, like Saudi Arabia and other regimes struggling with image problems. All it had to do was eliminate the narrators.

The Kim dynasty spent generations trying to control what its own people know about the outside world. Now it may have pulled off something just as remarkable: controlling what the outside world knows about North Korea.
